title: Cross-Contamination Prevention
blurb: How bacteria move between raw and ready-to-eat food, and the habits that stop it.
siteNotes: The venue's colour-coding scheme for boards, knives and equipment and where each is kept (your manager will show you).
Fridge layout and where raw meat and poultry are stored.
Where the handwash basins and sanitiser are.
legalNotes: Food businesses must prevent contamination and protect food, with hand hygiene and separation of raw and ready-to-eat food: Food Hygiene (England) Regulations 2013, with retained Regulation (EC) 852/2004. https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2013/2996
Store raw meat below ready-to-eat food so it cannot drip: Food Standards Agency guidance.

CHECK: colour-coding schemes vary. The trainer gives red for raw meat and green for salad and fruit "and so on". Many kitchens also use blue for raw fish, yellow for cooked meat, brown for vegetables and white for dairy and bakery; confirm the venue's scheme.

cards.title: Cross-Contamination Prevention
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- say what cross-contamination is and how it happens
- use separation, colour-coding and clean hands to stop it
- store raw meat below ready-to-eat food

cards.title: Bacteria on the move
cards.body:
Cross-contamination is one of the biggest causes of food poisoning. It happens when harmful bacteria (or allergens) are transferred from one food, surface or hand to another.

The classic example is juices from raw chicken getting onto a salad that will not be cooked. Cooking would have killed the bacteria on the chicken, but the salad goes out raw and makes someone ill.

cards.title: Keep raw and ready-to-eat apart
cards.body:
The main defence is separation: keep raw and ready-to-eat foods well apart at every stage.

Use the colour-coded chopping boards and equipment correctly. Never let a board or knife used for raw meat touch ready-to-eat food without a proper wash first.

cards.title: Clean hands, clean surfaces
cards.body:
Your hands are one of the most common ways bacteria travel around a kitchen, so wash them thoroughly and often.

Clean and sanitise surfaces and equipment between different tasks, and do not use the same cloth on raw-meat areas and then on a salad prep bench.

right.title: Do not
items: Reuse a cloth from raw meat on a salad bench
Use a raw-meat board for salad

cards.title: Raw below, ready-to-eat above
cards.body: Always keep raw meat and poultry stored below ready-to-eat foods in the fridge, so nothing can drip down and contaminate them.

items.title: Raw meat and poultry
items.text: Below, so juices cannot fall onto other food.

items.title: Ready-to-eat food
items.text: Top: nothing can drip onto it.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Keep raw and ready-to-eat foods well apart
- Use colour-coded boards and equipment correctly: red for raw meat, green for salad and fruit
- Wash your hands thoroughly and often
- Clean and sanitise between tasks, and never share a cloth across raw and salad areas
- Store raw meat and poultry below ready-to-eat food

cards.q: When must you wash your hands thoroughly in the kitchen?
options: Only at the end of a shift
cards.why: Wash thoroughly and often, especially after handling raw meat, taking out waste or touching your face.

cards.q: Why is raw chicken juice on a salad dangerous when it might be fine on a dish that is cooked?
options: Salad leaves are much harder to wash off
Chicken juice spoils the salad dressing
Cooked dishes always hold more bacteria
The salad is raw, so nothing kills the bacteria
cards.why: Cooking kills bacteria on the chicken or a cooked dish, but the salad goes out raw.
